Political Turmoil in Cambodia Disrupts Trade, Supply Chains Across Key Sectors

PHNOM PENH – Widespread anti-government protests and a government-imposed state of emergency in Cambodia have triggered major disruptions to trade, logistics, and economic activity across the country, prompting concern among business associations and international partners as the crisis enters its second week.

The unrest, sparked by allegations of irregularities in the June parliamentary elections, has led to mass demonstrations in Phnom Penh, Sihanoukville, and several provincial capitals. Security forces have established checkpoints on major highways, with the interior ministry confirming that at least 20 border crossings with Thailand and Vietnam have been closed “temporarily for public safety.” The move has effectively stalled cross-border movement of goods and people, with immediate impacts felt by exporters and manufacturers.

According to the Cambodia Freight Forwarders Association (CFFA), road freight volumes have dropped by an estimated 60% since the imposition of the state of emergency last Friday. “Truck convoys are stuck for days at border posts, with perishable goods at risk of spoilage,” said CFFA spokesperson Prak Samnang. “We are working with authorities to secure safe passage for essential goods, but the situation remains highly uncertain.”

The Association of Cambodian Garment Exporters (ACGE) reports that dozens of factories in the Phnom Penh Special Economic Zone and Kandal province have suspended operations due to supply shortages and worker absenteeism. “Our members are under tremendous pressure from buyers overseas to meet deadlines, but logistics are paralyzed,” said ACGE president Chenda Soth. “If this continues, many exporters risk losing contracts.”

The National Bank of Cambodia reported a 15% drop in daily cross-border remittance inflows since the unrest began. Local banks have shortened opening hours, citing staff safety and transportation difficulties. “Liquidity remains stable, but we are monitoring the situation closely,” said deputy governor Vann Channary.

Ports in Sihanoukville and Phnom Penh are operating at reduced capacity, with the Cambodia Port Operators Council confirming that vessel turnaround times have doubled. “Some shipping lines are rerouting cargo to Vietnamese ports until the situation stabilizes,” said council chair Hun Ratha.

Tourism, a key pillar of Cambodia’s economy, has also suffered, with the Ministry of Tourism recording a 70% drop in foreign arrivals week-on-week. Hotels and travel agencies report mass cancellations, especially in Siem Reap.

As the political standoff continues, business groups and foreign chambers of commerce are urging all parties to seek a peaceful resolution. “Economic stability is at risk,” said a joint statement by the Cambodia Business Roundtable. “We call for dialogue and the restoration of normalcy for the sake of livelihoods and investment.”
